newsitem.title: UK: Patten says Hong Kong people should run Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Patten says Hong Kong people should run Hong Kong.

text.p: Hong Kong's last British governor, Chris Patten, made no concessions to his Chinese successors on Thursday, declaring it was high time the people of the colony ran their own affairs.

In a hard-hitting interview with a British newspaper, The Independent, published four days before Hong Kong reverts to Chinese control, Patten castigated China's plans to roll back his democratic reforms.
"First of all, I believe that the things which are going to make Hong Kong survive are better long-term bets than authoritarianism or totalitarianism or Leninism or whatever you call it.
"Pluralism is the sound of the future in Asia and everywhere else."
Patten said he was leaving Hong Kong in good shape and all his Chinese-appointed successor, Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa, had to do when he took over on July 1 was "switch on the engine".
He added: "It is high time for Hong Kong people to run Hong Kong.

"I don't mean by that I want to walk away and say it's up to you; it's nothing to do with me, but ultimately the sort of place Hong Kong is, is the result of the sort of relationship Hong Kong people have with Peking.
"Maybe it would be easier to work that out when I am not around."
Patten also warned China not to use a heavy hand against any protests when it takes control of the colony.

"It's in everybody's interests to ensure that the arrangements for the handover are able to confirm Hong Kong's reputation for moderation and responsibility," he told the Financial Times in an interview.
Hong Kong pro-democracy activists have said they plan demonstrations over abolition of the current legislature and its replacement at midnight on Monday by a Beijing-appointed body.

Patten also warned that a decision by many European Union countries to send ministers to the Chinese ceremony to swear in the planned provisional legislature would further encourage China to disregard international pressure on human rights.
Europe "fell apart" earlier this year on a United Nations human rights resolution criticising China, and "it may well go in several different directions on this too," Patten said.
Britain was accused on Thursday of inviting contempt by deciding to attend the swearing-in of the controversial Beijing-appointed legislature.

After caving in to Beijing pressure to allow more troops into Hong Kong before the handover, Britain climbed down again on Wednesday and decided to join the United States in sending representatives to the ceremony.
"If they do this, they just invite contempt," pro-democracy legislator Emily Lau told Radio Hong Kong. "What kind of message are they trying to send to the rest of the world?"
